p.src:
Electrostatic forces require no new mechanics. If $U(\mathbf x)$ is a potential energy, then $\mathbf F=-\nabla U(\mathbf x),$ and the usual argument gives conservation of kinetic plus potential energy. For a particle of charge $e$ in an electrostatic potential $V(\mathbf x)$, $U(\mathbf x)=eV(\mathbf x),
  \qquad
  \mathbf F_{\mathrm{el}}=-e\nabla V.$ Magnetic forces have a different form. They depend on the particle’s velocity, so they cannot be introduced merely by adding another ordinary potential energy. Nevertheless, they do follow from an action principle and admit both Lagrangian and Hamiltonian descriptions. Reaching that description requires a short but essential interlude in vector calculus.

p.src: A field assigns a physical quantity to every point of space and, in general, to every time. Temperature and pressure are scalar fields. Wind velocity is a vector field. Electric and magnetic fields are vector fields. Other theories contain scalar fields even at microscopic scales, while gravitation is described by a tensor field. For the present discussion we suppress any time dependence and write fields as functions of $\mathbf x$.

p.src: The operational point of a field is locality. Imagine that a certain region is hidden inside a bag. To measure the electric field in that region, put a small test charge there and observe its acceleration. The force is determined by the field where the charge is located, not by a separate consultation with every distant source. The same statement applies to a magnetic field and a moving test charge. Later, the vector potential will force us to qualify this simple picture, but it is the right place to begin.

u.src: The derivative operator
en: The derivative operator

p.src:
Derivatives turn fields into other fields. We collect the three spatial derivatives into $\nabla
  =
  \left(
    \frac{\partial}{\partial x},
    \frac{\partial}{\partial y},
    \frac{\partial}{\partial z}
  \right).$ The symbol is read del or nabla. Its upside-down-triangle appearance is memorable, but its real significance is that it behaves formally like a vector whose components are differential operators.

p.src:
This is ordinary three-dimensional physical space, not phase space and not a many-particle configuration space. Moreover, $\nabla$ is not a vector field that can stand alone. It must act on something. If $T(\mathbf x)$ is a scalar temperature field, then $\nabla T
  =
  \left(
    \frac{\partial T}{\partial x},
    \frac{\partial T}{\partial y},
    \frac{\partial T}{\partial z}
  \right)$ is its gradient, a genuine vector field.

p.src: A scalar is not merely a quantity written with one component. It is a quantity whose value is independent of the orientation of the coordinate axes. Temperature is the standard example. Given a vector field $\mathbf E$, the local expression $\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf E$ is also a scalar. By contrast, constructing a potential by integrating a field is a nonlocal operation; it uses values along a path.

p.src: The cross product in components

u.src: The cross product in components
en: The cross product in components

p.src:
For two vectors $\mathbf V$ and $\mathbf A$, one component of the cross product is $(\mathbf V\times\mathbf A)_x
  =
  V_yA_z-V_zA_y.$ The other two follow by cycling $x\to y\to z\to x$. It is useful to replace $x,y,z$ by the indices $1,2,3$. The Kronecker symbol is $\delta_{ij}
  =
  \begin{cases}
    1,&i=j,\\
    0,&i\ne j,
  \end{cases}$ and the Levi–Civita symbol is defined by $\epsilon_{123}=\epsilon_{231}=\epsilon_{312}=1,
  \qquad
  \epsilon_{132}=\epsilon_{321}=\epsilon_{213}=-1,$ with $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$ whenever any two indices coincide. A cyclic ordering around a three-hour clock gives the plus signs; reversing the direction gives the minus signs. Interchanging any pair of indices reverses the sign, so $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is completely antisymmetric.

p.src:
We also use the summation convention: an index repeated in a term is summed from $1$ to $3$. The three cross-product equations then become $(\mathbf V\times\mathbf A)_i
  =
  \epsilon_{ijk}V_jA_k.$ For example, setting $i=1$ leaves only $(j,k)=(2,3)$ and $(3,2)$: $(\mathbf V\times\mathbf A)_1
  =
  \epsilon_{123}V_2A_3
  +\epsilon_{132}V_3A_2
  =
  V_2A_3-V_3A_2.$ The compact notation therefore contains exactly the familiar component rule.

p.src:
There is a second representation: $V_iA_j-V_jA_i
  =
  \epsilon_{ijk}(\mathbf V\times\mathbf A)_k.$ The left side has two indices and is antisymmetric under $i\leftrightarrow j$. As a matrix it has the pattern $M_{ij}
  =
  \begin{pmatrix}
    0&M_{12}&M_{13}\\
    -M_{12}&0&M_{23}\\
    -M_{13}&-M_{23}&0
  \end{pmatrix}.$ The diagonal entries vanish, and the lower triangle is fixed by the upper triangle. There are therefore three independent components.

p.src: Curl

u.src: Curl
en: Curl

p.src:
Replacing $\mathbf V$ by $\nabla$ defines the curl: $(\nabla\times\mathbf A)_i
  =
  \epsilon_{ijk}\frac{\partial A_k}{\partial x_j}.$ In ordinary components, $\begin{aligned}
  (\nabla\times\mathbf A)_x
  &=
  \frac{\partial A_z}{\partial y}
  -\frac{\partial A_y}{\partial z},\\
  (\nabla\times\mathbf A)_y
  &=
  \frac{\partial A_x}{\partial z}
  -\frac{\partial A_z}{\partial x},\\
  (\nabla\times\mathbf A)_z
  &=
  \frac{\partial A_y}{\partial x}
  -\frac{\partial A_x}{\partial y}.\end{aligned}$ Where divergence measures local spreading, curl measures local circulation. A fluid rotating around an axis has nonzero curl along that axis. The picture is particularly vivid for velocity fields, though the definition applies to any vector field.

u.src: Two Structural Identities
en: Two Structural Identities

p.src:
Two facts will do nearly all of the mathematical work: $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf A)=0,
  \qquad
  \nabla\times(\nabla s)=0.$ The first follows because the second derivatives are symmetric while $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is antisymmetric: $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf A)
  =
  \epsilon_{ijk}\partial_i\partial_j A_k
  =0.$ The second follows from equality of mixed partial derivatives: $\bigl[\nabla\times(\nabla s)\bigr]_i
  =
  \epsilon_{ijk}\partial_j\partial_k s
  =0.$

p.src:
These are the easy directions, suitable for the lecture’s promised homework or pop quiz. The converse statements require more care. Locally, or globally on an appropriate simply connected or contractible domain, $\begin{aligned}
  \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=0
  &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \mathbf F=\nabla\times\mathbf A,\\
  \nabla\times\mathbf F=0
  &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \mathbf F=\nabla s.\end{aligned}$ Without the domain qualification, holes and other global topological features can obstruct these conclusions. The lecture uses the local form, which is exactly what is needed below.

p.src: A magnetic field $\mathbf B$ is defined operationally through its effect on charged particles and currents. In ordinary electromagnetism without magnetic monopoles, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0.$ This differs from the electric field, whose divergence is proportional to electric charge density. Electric charges are sources and sinks of electric flux. No isolated source or sink of magnetic flux has been observed.

There is no local experiment of this classical kind that assigns a unique value to $\mathbf A$.

p.src: One Magnetic Field, Many Potentials

u.src: One Magnetic Field, Many Potentials
en: One Magnetic Field, Many Potentials

p.src:
Consider the simplest possible example, $\mathbf B=b\,\hat{\mathbf z},
  \qquad
  B_x=B_y=0,
  \qquad
  B_z=b,$ where $b$ is constant. One vector potential is $\mathbf A^{(1)}=(0,bx,0).$ Indeed, $(\nabla\times\mathbf A^{(1)})_z
  =
  \frac{\partial A_y^{(1)}}{\partial x}
  -\frac{\partial A_x^{(1)}}{\partial y}
  =b,$ and the other curl components vanish.

p.src:
This choice seems to single out the $y$-direction even though the physical field is rotationally symmetric in the $x$-$y$ plane. A second choice makes the arbitrariness explicit: $\mathbf A^{(2)}=(-by,0,0).$ It gives $(\nabla\times\mathbf A^{(2)})_z
  =
  0-\frac{\partial(-by)}{\partial y}
  =b.$ The two potentials differ by $\mathbf A^{(2)}-\mathbf A^{(1)}
  =
  (-by,-bx,0)
  =
  \nabla(-bxy).$ They are therefore gauge equivalent. A rotationally symmetric choice, $\mathbf A^{(\mathrm{sym})}
  =
  \frac12\,\mathbf B\times\mathbf r
  =
  \left(-\frac{by}{2},\frac{bx}{2},0\right),$ is another member of the same family.

p.src: The Lorentz Force

u.src: The Lorentz Force
en: The Lorentz Force

p.src:
We can now state the force law that the action principle must reproduce. In the conventions used here, $\boxed{
  \mathbf F
  =
  e\left(
    \mathbf E+\frac{\mathbf v}{c}\times\mathbf B
  \right)
  =
  -e\nabla V+\frac{e}{c}\mathbf v\times\mathbf B
  }.$ The symbol $e$ is the particle’s electric charge, $\mathbf v=\dot{\mathbf x}$ is its velocity, and $V$ is the scalar potential. The notation must not tempt us to confuse $V$ with $\mathbf v$. In SI language $V$ is measured in volts and $e$ in coulombs; the displayed $1/c$ belongs to the unit convention used in the lecture. The structural point is independent of units.

p.src: The electric and magnetic terms of the Lorentz force are displayed together. The magnetic contribution is proportional to $\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$.

caption.en: The electric and magnetic terms of the Lorentz force are displayed together. The magnetic contribution is proportional to $\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$.

p.src:
The electric term is conservative and already familiar. The magnetic term is new. It vanishes for a stationary particle and is perpendicular to both $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf B$. Consequently, $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf F_{\mathrm{mag}}
  =
  \frac{e}{c}\mathbf v\cdot(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)
  =0.$ A static magnetic field bends a trajectory but does no work on the particle. This is unlike viscous drag, which is directed opposite the velocity and removes kinetic energy.

p.src: Historically, forces on current-carrying wires were known before the force on an individual charge was isolated. Lorentz recognized that the wire force could be understood by assigning the velocity-dependent term to each moving charge. The complete electric-plus-magnetic expression is now called the Lorentz force law, although the magnetic piece is the novel part in the present discussion.

p.src: The Coriolis analogy

u.src: The Coriolis analogy
en: The Coriolis analogy

p.src:
We have seen a velocity crossed with a fixed vector before. In a frame rotating with angular velocity $\boldsymbol\omega$, the Coriolis force can be written $\mathbf F_{\mathrm{Cor}}
  =
  2m\,\mathbf v\times\boldsymbol\omega.$ It has the same algebraic form as the magnetic force: $2m\boldsymbol\omega
  \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
  \frac{e}{c}\mathbf B.$ A uniform magnetic field perpendicular to a plane therefore bends charged-particle trajectories in much the same way that a rotating frame deflects moving bodies.

p.src: The analogy can be pushed into a small thought experiment. On a rotating platform, a suitable electrostatic field can cancel the centrifugal term for a chosen particle, while a suitable uniform magnetic field can cancel the Coriolis term. The cancellation works only for a chosen charge-to-mass ratio: electric and magnetic forces scale with $e$, whereas the inertial forces scale with $m$. A field arrangement tuned for electrons would not cancel the same terms for particles with a different $e/m$.

p.src:
For a trajectory $\mathbf x(t)$, write $S[\mathbf x]
  =
  \int_{t_i}^{t_f}L(\mathbf x,\dot{\mathbf x},t)\,dt.$ The lecture uses the same handwritten letter for the action and the vector potential, but we use $S$ for the action and $\mathbf A$ for the vector potential. The physical path makes $S$ stationary under variations that hold both endpoints fixed. The traditional phrase least action is convenient, though stationary action is more accurate because the extremum need not be a minimum.

p.src: Gauge Transformations Change Only the Endpoints

u.src: Gauge Transformations Change Only the Endpoints
en: Gauge Transformations Change Only the Endpoints

p.src:
Now perform the gauge transformation $A_i\longmapsto A_i+\partial_i s.$ The action changes by $\begin{aligned}
  \Delta S
  &=
  \frac{e}{c}\int_\gamma \partial_i s\,dx_i\\
  &=
  \frac{e}{c}\int_\gamma ds\\
  &=
  \frac{e}{c}
  \left[
    s(\mathbf x_f)-s(\mathbf x_i)
  \right].\end{aligned}$ Each infinitesimal segment contributes the value of $s$ at one end minus its value at the other. On summing, all interior contributions cancel telescopically, leaving only the two endpoints.
